mcqs.question: Why does the location feed typically need a separate, high-throughput store from the ride/trip data?
options: Ride/trip records require faster writes than driver location pings
Location updates are far higher in write volume than ride events, but each individual update is disposable once superseded
Regulations require driver location and trip data to be stored in different countries
The matching engine cannot read from more than one datastore at a time
mcqs.explanation: Location pings vastly outnumber ride state changes and only the latest position matters, making it a high-write, low-durability workload — the opposite profile of trip records, which are low-volume but must persist reliably. There's no such regulatory or single-datastore constraint implied here.

mcqs.question: What is the main risk of storing live driver locations and durable trip records in the same database with the same durability guarantees?
options: You either overpay for durability on the extremely high-volume location feed, or underpay for it on records that need to persist reliably
It becomes impossible to query either dataset
The API surface would need twice as many endpoints
Drivers would be unable to go offline
mcqs.explanation: The core mismatch is durability and volume: forcing one durability model onto both means the ephemeral, high-volume location feed pays for guarantees it doesn't need, or the durable trip records get shortchanged on guarantees they do need. The other options aren't real consequences of this choice.

mcqs.question: What does marketplace-aware matching trade off against pure nearest-driver matching?
options: It removes the need for a location index entirely
It guarantees every rider gets the closest possible driver
It eliminates surge pricing as a concept
It accepts a small added delay per match in exchange for better average outcomes across all riders and drivers
mcqs.explanation: Considering heading, ETA, or holding a decision briefly to weigh multiple riders/drivers together costs a bit of latency on any single match, but can meaningfully improve the marketplace-wide outcome. It still needs a location index, doesn't guarantee closest-driver-always, and is unrelated to surge pricing.

mcqs.question: When does batched matching earn its added latency over greedy nearest-match?
options: When a dense spike creates many simultaneous riders and drivers, so a global assignment can meaningfully beat first-come-first-served
Only when there is exactly one rider and one driver available
Never — greedy matching is always strictly better for every scenario
Only in low-density areas with rare overlapping requests
mcqs.explanation: Batching pays off when there are enough concurrent riders and drivers to actually choose between alternative assignments — a demand spike, not a quiet period. In low-density or single-match scenarios there's nothing to optimize, so greedy is preferable there instead.

mcqs.question: Why can the closest driver by straight-line GPS distance still be a bad match?
options: Straight-line distance ignores the road network, driver heading, and traffic, all of which can make a farther driver arrive sooner
GPS coordinates are never accurate enough to compare two drivers
The closest driver is always already on another trip
Straight-line distance can't be computed in real time at scale
mcqs.explanation: A driver who looks closest on a map can be heading away from the pickup or blocked by road topology, giving them a worse real ETA than someone farther away but better positioned. GPS accuracy and computability aren't the issue, and there's no rule that the closest driver is always mid-trip.
